title: A little girl looked up. The experts called her father a fraud.

post.caption: Altamira, Spain: the cave paintings a little girl spotted in 1879 — and the experts who refused to believe them. Images: public domain.

beats.text: A little girl looked up. The experts called her father a fraud.
1879, northern Spain. An amateur scientist, Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, was digging in a cave near his home.
beats.say: Eighteen seventy-nine, northern Spain. An amateur scientist, Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, was digging in a cave near his home.

beats.text: His little daughter María wandered deeper inside. She looked up and shouted: Papa, bulls!
The ceiling was covered in bison. Red, black and ochre, painted over the bumps of the rock so they seem to breathe.
He published his find. Europe's experts laughed. Far too good for cavemen, they said. A forgery.
Sautuola died in 1888, still called a fraud.
beats.say: Sautuola died in eighteen eighty-eight, still called a fraud.

beats.text: In 1902, the leading sceptic, Émile Cartailhac, published an apology. Its title: Mea culpa of a sceptic.
beats.say: In nineteen-oh-two, the leading sceptic, Émile Cartailhac, published an apology. Its title: Mea culpa of a sceptic.

beats.text: Today we know some marks in Altamira are over thirty-five thousand years old.
The cave is so fragile that only five visitors a week may enter, chosen by lottery.
